title: Titty-Tat, the circus trumpeter playing bop in the 1920s
summary: They recall a circus trumpeter nicknamed Titty-Tat (Steele) who played boppish phrases forty years early; Allen compares it to flatted fifths in 1929 records.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And then we had Titty-Tat a while. Yeah, Tatt. What's Titty-Tat right now? Now, that's a man was playing bop on the trumpet in the 20s. He was, how many years, about 40 years ahead of time.

Oh, Titty-Tat. I can think of his name. Where is he from? New Orleans. No, Titty-Tat, Titty-Tat's from New Orleans. Oh, Titty-Tat. I'm talking about Titty-Tat. The trumpet. The trumpet was living on Mount Main. Hot doggie. Used to keep the name. Yeah, he played it upside down. And then he used to play that Titty-Tit-Tat, you know, that box trumpet. In other words. 40 years ago. He was on a circus type. Yeah, it was a circus type. A circus type playing. Yes, sir. He came off a circus and came with us. That man could go. And then once we had this fella, used to play with Trent's orchestra playing tenor with us once too, you know. With Alphonse? With Trent, yeah, with the big orchestra. I forget the, I can't think of the fella's name, though, but he was humbling. Steele. Steele was his last name. Steele was his last name. Steele was his last name. Yeah, we used to call him Titty-Tat, because that's what he used to make out of the trumpet all the time. You know, like that. Sometimes he'd play, he'd take a chorus, they'd take a chorus, he'd play, maybe put in some of that circus music in it, you know. Yeah.

Yeah. Red Island was playing a lot of flatted fifths back in 1929. I got records of that and all that stuff, you know. Higginbotham Blues, the ends of a flatted fifth in 1929. That's what J.C. Higginbotham was playing. He was out of that Louis Russell group, you know.
